title: What Happens During an HVAC Tune-Up?
h1: What Happens During an HVAC Tune-Up?
description: An HVAC tune-up checks controls, electrical parts, coils, drains, airflow and safety on your heating and cooling. Here's what a technician looks at and why.
quick_answer: During an HVAC tune-up, a technician checks the thermostat, tightens and tests electrical parts, inspects and cleans coils, flushes the condensate drain, checks airflow and the filter, and confirms the system heats and cools properly. On a gas furnace, they also inspect burners, the flame sensor, venting and safety controls.
body:
A tune-up is a scheduled checkup for your heating and cooling system. It doesn't promise your system won't break, but it gives a technician the chance to find loose connections, dirty parts, weak components and drain problems while the system is still running.

When should you schedule a tune-up?

In San Diego and Orange County, the best time to check the AC is spring, before inland heat sets in. Furnaces are best checked in fall, before cold nights. Many homeowners combine both into one visit a year, which works well in our mild climate.

Scheduling early also helps you avoid the rush. When the first heat wave hits, everyone calls at once.

What does a technician check on the cooling side?

  • Thermostat. Confirm it reads correctly and that the system starts, runs and stops in the right sequence.
  • Electrical connections. Tighten terminals and look for burned or corroded wiring.
  • Capacitors and contactor. Test capacitors, which help motors start, and check the contactor for pitting or wear.
  • Motors. Check the outdoor fan and indoor blower motors for proper operation and current draw.
  • Outdoor coil. Clean dirt, leaves and debris. Near the coast, look for corrosion from salt air.
  • Indoor coil. Inspect for dirt and growth, which restrict airflow.
  • Condensate drain. Flush the line and check the pan and any safety switch, especially for attic units.
  • Refrigerant performance. Measure pressures and temperatures to see if the system is operating within the manufacturer's specifications.
  • Temperature split. Compare the air going in to the air coming out.

What does a technician check on a furnace?

  • Burners and ignition. Check the igniter and look at how the burners light.
  • Flame sensor. Clean it if needed. A dirty sensor is a common reason furnaces light and then shut off.
  • Heat exchanger. Inspect what's visible for cracks, rust or other concerns.
  • Venting. Make sure the flue is connected, sloped correctly and not blocked.
  • Safety controls. Test limit switches and the pressure switch.
  • Gas connections. Look for proper connections and operation.
  • Carbon monoxide. Many technicians check for carbon monoxide around the furnace and in the home.

Heat pumps get a similar electrical and coil check, plus a test of heating mode and the reversing valve.

What can you do before the tune-up?

A few minutes of prep makes the visit more useful:

  1. Replace or check the filter, and note its size.
  2. Clear a path to the furnace or air handler, especially in the attic or garage.
  3. Clear plants and stored items away from the outdoor unit.
  4. Write down any problems you've noticed, like hot rooms, noises, odors, short cycling or high bills.
  5. Have the age of the system handy if you know it.

What should you get after the tune-up?

You should get a clear summary of what was checked, what was cleaned and anything that needs attention. A good technician will explain which issues are urgent, which can wait and which are just worth watching. You should never feel pressured to agree to a repair on the spot.

If something needs repair, ask why, what happens if you wait and what it would cost. A written estimate makes it easier to decide.

What problems do tune-ups commonly find?

Most findings are small, which is the point of catching them early. Common ones include:

  • A weak capacitor that could leave the outdoor unit unable to start on a hot day
  • A slow or partly clogged drain line
  • A dirty flame sensor causing the furnace to shut off
  • Loose or corroded electrical connections
  • A dirty outdoor coil, especially after windy weather
  • Torn duct insulation or a disconnected duct near the equipment
  • A filter that's the wrong size or hasn't been changed

Is a yearly tune-up worth it?

For most homes, yes. Regular maintenance helps catch weak parts before they fail on the hottest or coldest day, keeps the system running efficiently and gives you a record of the system's condition. Many equipment manufacturers also expect regular maintenance as part of their warranty terms, so keep your service records.

Learn more about maintenance and repairs on our HVAC services page, or look at current specials on tune-ups.
faqs: How long does an HVAC tune-up take?
Most tune-ups take about an hour or two per system, depending on the equipment, access and condition. Attic units and systems that need extra cleaning can take longer.
How often should I get an HVAC tune-up?
Once a year works for most homes in our area. Systems that run hard, like those in hot inland areas, or homes with both a furnace and AC that see heavy use may benefit from a spring and a fall visit.
Will a tune-up fix my AC problem?
A tune-up can solve simple problems like a dirty coil or clogged drain. If a part has failed, the technician will explain what's needed and give you an estimate for the repair.
Does a tune-up include adding refrigerant?
Checking refrigerant performance is part of the visit, but adding refrigerant usually isn't. A system low on refrigerant has a leak, and the right fix is finding and repairing it.
